text: Everything this chapter has covered so far assumes a person is sitting at a keyboard or holding a phone. Service accounts, scripts, and backend applications have no human behind them in the moment they authenticate, so they need an entirely different authentication model — one this lesson walks through, along with the real risk of long-lived credentials and why short-lived ones have become the standard.

A service account is the oldest, crudest non-human login — often just a username and a password or key an application uses to act. An API key is a static secret string sent with each request, simple to use but just as simple to leak since it's usually the same value for the life of the integration. A managed identity is issued and rotated automatically by the cloud platform itself, so there's no secret for a developer to store or copy. A workload identity generalizes that further: a short-lived token issued to a container, CI job, or function based on a trust relationship, not a long-term credential handed out once.

The risk profile is stark. A static API key pasted into a config file can stay valid for years — exploitable the entire time it sits leaked in a repository, a chat message, or a forgotten script, until someone manually finds and revokes it. A workload identity token, by contrast, is valid for about an hour and rotates automatically. If it leaks, the exposure window closes on its own, often before anyone even notices.

None of the human-facing authentication this chapter covered applies here. There's no password for a non-human identity to type, no phone to receive a push, no FIDO2 key to tap. Instead, trust comes from the platform itself — attestation and federation stand in for the human decision point that simply doesn't exist for a script or a service.
That closes out authentication architecture. Chapter 3 turns to authorization — once an identity is proven, what is it actually allowed to do — starting with RBAC design for a real organization.
